platforms.title: If Your Ear Feels Clogged and Sore, Check These Habits
platforms.meta_description: Ear feeling clogged and sore isn't random — untreated colds, plane pressure changes, and smoke exposure can each block the eustachian tube and trap bacteria.
platforms.body_html:
A clogged, throbbing ear is easy to write off as just a bad day, but it's often the result of specific habits blocking the eustachian tube — the passage connecting your ear and nose — creating conditions where bacteria can thrive. Three habits in particular raise this risk.

What Actually Happens When the Eustachian Tube Blocks

The most common culprit is leaving a cold or rhinitis untreated for days. Research shows viral upper respiratory infections inflame tissue around the eustachian tube and impair its function, and as negative pressure builds in the middle ear, secretions and bacteria from the nose get pulled in toward it. The longer that inflammation lingers, the longer the tube stays blocked, and the more secretions accumulate with nowhere to drain.

Second is not swallowing or yawning during takeoff and landing on a flight. Medical sources like Mayo Clinic explain that outside pressure changes rapidly during ascent and descent, and if the eustachian tube doesn't open in time, the middle ear becomes a near-vacuum, pulling on the eardrum and causing the lining to swell and secretions to pool. Third is frequent exposure to cigarette smoke. Whether it's direct smoking or ongoing secondhand exposure at home, cigarette smoke steadily damages the tiny hair-like cilia lining the eustachian tube that would normally sweep secretions back out — and household smoking is a well-documented risk factor for otitis media in children.

What Actually Helps Protect the Eustachian Tube

First, if a cold or rhinitis drags on for more than a few days, don't just wait it out — treat it early. Saline rinses or a prescribed nasal spray to bring inflammation down quickly is the first step toward protecting eustachian tube function. Second, chew gum or swallow frequently during takeoff and landing, and open your mouth wide like you're yawning if you need to. That motion actively opens the tube and reduces the pressure difference. Third, avoid cigarette smoke, direct or secondhand. If you smoke, quitting is the clearest fix, and if someone in your household smokes, simply keeping it strictly outdoors makes a real difference on its own.

How you blow your nose matters more than you'd think, too. Blocking both nostrils at once and blowing hard spikes the pressure inside your nose, and that spike can push secretions and bacteria straight toward the eustachian tube. Blowing one nostril at a time, gently rather than forcefully, cuts that risk down — this small change in technique matters even more while you actually have an active cold or nasal congestion.

If tackling all three at once feels like too much, start by thinking back to your last clogged-ear episode — was it right after a bad cold, or shortly after a long flight? If the pain is severe, fever shows up, or fluid drains from the ear, don't try to manage all of that on your own at home — book an appointment with an ENT doctor and let them check the eardrum directly rather than guessing from symptoms alone.
